title: A superscript "\u00b2" says isdigit() but int() refuses it
assumption: If isdigit() returns True (or a /\d/ regex matches), the value is safe to pass to a numeric parser.

input.description: Fullwidth letters pasted from CJK input methods, a superscript exponent copied from a web page into a quantity field, or a ligature character from a PDF copy-paste landing in a filename or search box.

what_goes_wrong: "\u00b2".isdigit() is True, but int("\u00b2") raises ValueError; meanwhile fullwidth "\uff46\uff4f\uff4f" does not equal "foo" and the 3-character ligature "\ufb01le" has length 4 after normalization even though no character was literally inserted.
why: Python's str.isdigit() is true for any character whose Numeric_Type is Digit or Decimal, which includes superscript and subscript digits, but int() only accepts Numeric_Type=Decimal (General_Category Nd) characters, so isdigit() cannot predict whether int() will succeed; str.isdecimal() is the check that matches int(). NFKC (UAX #15) replaces compatibility characters, such as fullwidth letters, ligatures and superscripts, with their ordinary equivalents, which is why NFKC turns "\u00b2" into "2" and makes the fullwidth string equal "foo". It does not fix every case: ETHIOPIC DIGIT ONE (U+1369) is isdigit() but not isdecimal(), has no compatibility decomposition, and still fails int() after NFKC. A single compatibility character can also expand: "\ufb01" (the fi ligature) becomes two letters, so the 3-code-point "\ufb01le" normalizes to 4.

repros.code:
import unicodedata
sup = "\u00b2"
print(sup.isdigit(), sup.isdecimal())
try:
    int(sup)
except ValueError as e:
    print("ValueError")
n = unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", sup)
print(n, n.isdecimal(), int(n))

fullwidth = "\uff46\uff4f\uff4f"
print(fullwidth == "foo", unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", fullwidth) == "foo")

lig = "\ufb01le"
print(len(lig), len(unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", lig)))
repros.expected_output:
True False
ValueError
2 True 2
False True
3 4

fix: Normalize untrusted text with NFKC at the input boundary before validating it as an identifier, filename, or number, and when checking "is this parseable as an integer" use str.isdecimal() in Python (not isdigit()) or attempt-and-catch the parse — never trust isdigit()/regex \d alone to predict int()/Number() success.

sources.title: Unicode Standard Annex #15: Unicode Normalization Forms (NFKC)

test_cases.note: A strict integer parser should reject this (Python's int() raises ValueError) even though isdigit() returns True; validate with isdecimal() or attempt-and-catch, or NFKC-normalize first if you intend to accept it as 2.
